figures.title: The table is a lookup, not an ordering
figures.caption: The lookup is one gather. The id arrives as an integer with no geometry, indexes E — a table of V rows, each d_model wide — and the gather returns one row, the chapter's king row (0.8, 0.1), which becomes x in the residual stream. No arithmetic mixes rows, and nothing in the id is ordered: it records when a BPE merge happened.
figures.alt: Four stages left to right, then wrapping. The id for king arrives as an integer with no geometry. That integer indexes E, a table of V rows of width d_model. The gather returns exactly one row, (0.8, 0.1). That row becomes x, the vector the block stack reads at this position.

nodes: id for king: an integer, a merge rank
x: width d_model, into the residual stream

steps.label: A BPE id arrives as an integer. It is a merge rank, so it carries no geometry.
The integer is an offset into E, which has V rows of width d_model.
The gather returns exactly one row, (0.8, 0.1); no arithmetic mixes rows.
That row becomes x, the residual stream's input at this position.

figures.title: Same two rows, before and after the shared component comes out
figures.caption: The chapter's two rows drawn as rays from one origin, at the same scale. Before centering they sit close together and score cosine 0.917: the anisotropic cone. Subtract the table mean m = (1, 1) and the same rows both shrink and separate, scoring 0.166. All-but-the-Top does the rest: remove each centered vector's projection onto the top principal components.
figures.alt: Two square plots sharing one scale. Left, raw rows from a common origin: a points to (1.6, 1.05) and b to (1.05, 1.6), nearly the same direction, with an arc between them and cos 0.917 printed beneath the plot. The mean m = (1, 1) is drawn as a dashed ray on the left plot and named in the same line. Right, after subtracting m = (1, 1): a prime points to (0.6, 0.05) and b prime to (0.05, 0.6), much shorter and almost perpendicular, with an arc between them and cos 0.166 beneath the plot. Both plots print their coordinates; a shared note explains that the drop from 0.917 to 0.166 is the cone coming out.

data.note: Both rows score 0.917 before centering because the table sits in a narrow cone. Taking out the shared component drops the same pair to 0.166.

anim.intro: Press Play or Next to watch the shared component come out.

steps.label: Two unrelated rows, a = (1.6, 1.05) and b = (1.05, 1.6): nearly the same ray.
Subtract the table mean m = (1, 1) from both rows.
a′ = (0.6, 0.05) and b′ = (0.05, 0.6): shorter, and almost perpendicular.
Cosine falls from 0.917 to 0.166. That drop is the cone coming out.

figures.title: Tying saves a second copy of the embedding matrix
figures.caption: Tying sets W = Eᵀ, so one V × d_model matrix serves both the input lookup and the output projection. GPT-2 small publishes 124M parameters with the matrix counted once; untied, the same model carries a second 38,597,376-number copy, about 163M, so tying saves roughly 24 percent of the untied count.
figures.alt: Four boxes left to right: token id (one integer), gather row k of E (row, width 768), h, width d (residual stream), and logits: h Eᵀ (one score per token). An accent lane runs above the boxes from the lookup to the logits, labelled W = Eᵀ: the output projection is the same matrix, read the other way. The note prints 50,257 × 768 = 38,597,376 numbers stored once, and that untying stores a second copy, 124M + 38.6M ≈ 163M.
